intro.heading: Three pages, three different readers
intro.body: Most emergencies are not the end of anything. They are a week where you cannot be reached, or ten minutes to get out of the house, or a sitter holding a phone that goes to voicemail. The information someone needs in that week is not complicated. It is just scattered — a pediatrician in one phone, a policy in a drawer, a neighbour's number nobody wrote down, and the answer to where the birth certificates are living entirely in your head.

features.title: The fridge page
features.body: Contacts, medical essentials, animals, shut-offs. It holds nothing that would be dangerous in a kitchen, which is why it can live where a stranger will find it.

features.title: The page you hand over
features.body: For a sitter, a neighbour, or a relative staying while you are away. Everything they need, and nothing that would matter if they kept it.

features.title: The ten-minute list
features.body: What to carry out and in what order, with where each thing is. Print it twice - one for a closet door, one for the car.

screens.caption: Who has a key, who can collect a child, who lives close enough to arrive.

screens.captionBold: Where it is, never what it says.
screens.caption: Have it, need it, or not applicable - with where the original lives and who else can reach it.
People and animals, then papers, then prescriptions - arranged by what cannot be replaced.

privacy.heading: Private by design, not by promise
privacy.body: Nothing you type ever leaves your device. It never asks for a Social Security number, an account number, a policy number, a password, or a PIN — there is nowhere in it to put one. That is deliberate: it is what makes the printed pages safe to leave on a fridge or hand to a babysitter.

cards.title: Why this one is deliberately incomplete
cards.body: An emergency binder is meant to be found — on a fridge, in a sitter's hand, by whoever arrives first. That is exactly why this one records where things are and who to call, and never account numbers, Social Security numbers, passwords or codes. There is nowhere in it to put them. A binder complete enough to be dangerous is a binder you cannot leave out, which defeats its purpose.

cards.title: Zero network requests
cards.body: The app is a single file that runs entirely in your browser, on your device. It makes no connections and loads nothing from the internet. You can run it with Wi-Fi off. The file itself isn't encrypted or password-protected — but by design it holds nothing that would be dangerous in the wrong hands, which is exactly what makes an unlocked binder acceptable.

cards.title: Never a password
cards.body: By design, it never asks for or stores passwords or PINs. It records that accounts exist and where your written instructions live — the map, never the keys.

cards.title: Yours forever
cards.body: One-time purchase. The file is yours, works offline for life, and will still open years from now, exactly as it does today.

crossSell.heading: Already had the fire, the flood, or the break-in?
crossSell.body: Pairs with the Home Inventory & Insurance Claim Organizer: this covers the ten minutes before you leave, that one covers proving what you owned once you are allowed back. The Estate Planning Organizer is the natural next step rather than an alternative — this is the one people actually finish, and finishing it is usually when they notice the larger job is still waiting.
